# Review disposition — state probe

Date:2026-11-22. Plan approved by root and execution peer before implementation.
No native database experiment executed by this lane at this checkpoint.

## Peer changes accepted

- Historical effect replay returns the immutable original receipt after cutover,
  with exact authority/schema and PostgreSQL JSONB semantic-value comparison.
  A new stale effect remains rejected. After uniqueness contention, the receiver
  performs a fresh statement lookup and validates the winner.
- Publication lock order is attempt→head; effect order is head→effect. Same-attempt
  publishers serialize before CAS and return the same terminal outcome.
- Artifact A may be selected again as fresh live A2, never the old A1 identity.
  S04 independently exercises stale publication revision, epoch and generation.
- Fault child checkpoint wait now rejects on early exit/error, kills after a
  bounded timeout, and cannot leave an unused-mode rejection unhandled.
- Scenario setup failures are recorded. S08 is explicitly a held raw SQL lock
  schedule plus inspected receiver composition; no hook executes guest code inside
  a transaction.

## Root source review

The root reviewed the fixture, child and12 DB scenarios. Read Committed
reconciliation, lock ordering, historical receipt handling, S12 visibility and
FK controls were accepted in principle. Native execution remains gated on the
frozen shared-backend source/hash review. The protected effect is the inserted
database row; this fixture does not claim atomicity with arbitrary external
business effects. S10 remains a quiescent toy codec admission counterexample.

## Compiler disposition

Exact TypeScript7.0.2; strict/noUncheckedIndexedAccess/exactOptionalPropertyTypes,
noEmit, skipLibCheck=false. Initial check failed3 times because pg query parameter
arrays were marked readonly. Fresh parameter arrays now use mutable unknown[];
no cast, compiler suppression or weaker configuration was introduced. The
initial and successful reviewed logs are retained separately.

The shared input then added9 execution-lane TS files and Resources0.2.2 to the
same package/lock. Its first strict check found2 Worker narrowing errors, retained
in `typecheck-shared-initial.log`. The execution owner added a checked record type
predicate and read the actual private exit receipt after the asynchronous native
callback. The second shared check passed with unchanged strictness. Runtime input
has15 files and aggregate SHA256
`d8e90b0e58cd496ebfceb3b489dafaf795d0b65727a5a9370845de576bc344f9`.

Only the execution lane is authorized to run3 local non-DB Worker cases. Root
owns the hosted PostgreSQL18.7 run. The image selected by root is
`postgres:18.7-bookworm@sha256:194e55feb2597b1465dbee81cc9fd8d204566cd2eb42c8d22fd6c931a38781b1`;
this is planned runtime identity, not observed server evidence at this checkpoint.

Counts:12 DB scenarios; S09 is the joint real Worker/DB scenario owned by the
execution lane. It must not be counted twice when combining reports.

# Native state/publication/recovery probe — plan before execution

Date: 2026-11-22, Europe/Kiev. Status: root and execution peer reviewed 2026-11-22; implementation approved; no native
PostgreSQL execution yet. This extends the prior native ALS/Yjs/browser evidence
with the actual state receiver and independently connected controllers.

## Boundary and reuse

Use a disposable real PostgreSQL **18.7** service (supported release published
2026-11-12), the released node-postgres driver with an exact verified pin, Node
24.22.3 and strict TypeScript 7.0.2. PostgreSQL 19.0 is newer; this deliberately
qualifies one supported 18.x profile, not every version. Record actual server
version/image identity and all installed package identities. No ORM, migration
framework, lock service, WAL or durable workflow engine is implemented.

The database adapter is a **test host's narrow authority fixture**, not a new
public library or replacement for an application's existing canonical store.
PostgreSQL owns transactions, uniqueness, row locks and crash rollback. One
checked-out client owns each transaction; no transaction uses pool.query.
Candidate/plugin code never executes inside these transactions.

The selected integration mode allows A's admitted computation/stream to finish
on A's retained implementation after B publishes, but fences new A commits to
shared mutable state. This is an explicit mode. It does not prescribe that all
long-lived operations lose write permission during every kind of update.

## Experimental seam

Publication/durable-attempt and shared-effect receiver are separate concerns:

- `readHead()` returns generation, monotonic publication revision, effect epoch
  and immutable cohort ID. These identities are separate; this strict-cutover
  fixture advances both revision and effect epoch on publication.
- `admitAttempt({attemptId, expectedRevision, expectedGeneration,
  targetGeneration, cohortDigest, baselineId})` durably records exact inputs.
  Reusing an ID with different inputs is rejected. Replaying the same inputs
  returns the existing attempt, including its selected baseline.
- `publishAttempt(attemptId)` uses the recorded expected head and returns a
  durable committed/conflict outcome in the same transaction as head mutation.
- `observeAttempt(attemptId)` returns recorded pending/committed/conflict or
  absent/unknown. An absent row is not evidence that external effects never ran.
- `guardedWrite({effectId, generation, effectEpoch, stateSchema, value})` checks the actual
  authority row and commits the effect under the same receiver transaction.
  Same key/different payload or authority is rejected. Replaying an already committed effect after cutover returns its original receipt without a new write; a new stale effect is rejected. The receiver rechecks the committed receipt after unique-key contention with a fresh statement snapshot.

Revisions and effect epochs cross the fixture boundary as decimal strings, not
lossy JS numbers. State schema, live generation, artifact/cohort and publication
revision are independent contract axes; a future compatible-write mode may
preserve an effect epoch across a code publication.
Cohort IDs are inert values supplied by the caller; no dependency grammar or
graph planner is recreated. Lock order: publication takes attempt then head; effects take head then effect. Publication serializes same-attempt callers before CAS; the second observes the original terminal result. No transaction path inverts these locks. Test-only synchronization hooks and raw clients are
kept out of these feature seams.

## Oracles and synchronization

Use explicit inter-process messages and database-visible lock waits
(`pg_blocking_pids`/`pg_stat_activity`) to establish ordering. A sleep is never
the only evidence that concurrent work started or was blocked. Every case has
a bounded timeout and finally cleanup of only its own clients/processes/schema.
No load/throughput conclusion is drawn from these schedules. The deliberately
held FOR SHARE lock is a test barrier; production SQL critical sections must be
bounded and contain no plugin callback or awaited Worker computation.

| ID | Decisive native case | Independent outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S01 | Two connections capture the same expected head and race B versus C | Exactly one CAS publication succeeds; one conflicts; head revision advances once; both durable outcomes are coherent |
| S02 | Two connections concurrently submit the same attempt and publication | One durable attempt, one head advance, identical terminal outcome on replay |
| S03 | Same attempt ID with changed target, baseline or expected revision | Explicit mismatch; original immutable inputs/outcome remain unchanged |
| S04 | A1 → B1 → A2 distinct live generations, artifact/human label A reused; stale request from A1 | Monotonic publication revision and separate effect epoch reject stale publication/write despite repeated human/artifact label |
| S05 | Controller child commits publication, then exits before sending the application reply; fresh child/controller reconciles | Recorded outcome and head agree; same-attempt retry adds no publication/effect; claim is lost application reply, not a simulated lost PostgreSQL wire COMMIT acknowledgement or reconstructed Worker readiness |
| S06 | Controller child holds uncommitted head/outcome changes and is killed | Backend rollback leaves old head and no committed receipt; fresh controller can continue using the already recorded attempt |
| S07 | Negative control: old writer uses FOR KEY SHARE on non-key head revision; B publishes before A commits | Actual late old write succeeds, demonstrating that this weaker lock is not the required fence |
| S08 | Positive control: old writer holds FOR SHARE through its state effect; B publisher contends | Native lock wait is observed; A commits before B publication; after B publishes, a new A write is rejected |
| S09 | A worker exits after a request was dispatched to the parent-owned sink; release that delayed request after B publishes | Guarded sink rejects stale A; separate explicitly unsafe sink accepts it, proving worker termination is not external-effect rollback |
| S10 | New writer stores a v2-only state variant; old decoder attempts read/write after code rollback | Actual old decoder rejects incompatible state; guarded rollback admission is denied; the expanded compatible writer profile remains readable by both |
| S11 | Durable attempt records baseline S0; controller dies; S1 appears; same attempt resumes | Resumed attempt retains S0; a genuinely new attempt may select S1 |
| S12 | Concurrent INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING + same-statement fallback SELECT encounters another uncommitted insert | Negative-control statement may return no row after the conflict commits; a fresh statement observes the winner; no missing receipt is mislabeled as absent authority |
| S13 | Artifact metadata deletion races a new retained-reference insertion with native FK restriction | No dangling committed canonical reference; identify which transaction succeeds. This does not prove physical object-store deletion or full runtime retention |

S09 is joint integration with the execution lane; it must use real Workers and
the real database effect sink, not only model counters. S10 uses explicit
consumer codecs and disposable JSONB state; a toy codec counterexample does not
qualify arbitrary production schema migrations.

## Evidence and scope

Preserve the pre-execution plan, exact sources/locks/configuration, installation
and strict-compiler logs, actual server identity, test output and machine-readable
observations, all failures and source hashes. Parent owns hosted workflow,
publication and immediate push. Native execution starts only after review.

Estimated fixture/integration code: 500–850 lines; tests/oracles/fault-child:
350–650 lines; research/configuration/evidence: 150–300 lines. No production code
is adopted. Design confidence 8/10, bounded achievable reliability 8/10,
complexity 6/10. These are planning judgments, not availability measurements.

Unqualified: PostgreSQL failover/power loss, distributed replica linearizability,
external network effects, generic workflow replay, every isolation level,
performance/overload bounds, arbitrary migration reversibility and production
library admission.

## Primary source basis already read

- PostgreSQL 18 explicit locking:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/explicit-locking.html
- PostgreSQL 18 isolation/Read Committed:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html
- PostgreSQL 18 INSERT/ON CONFLICT:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-insert.html
- PostgreSQL 18.7 released version:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18-7.html
- node-postgres transaction ownership:
  https://node-postgres.com/features/transactions

Exact source/tag/package identities and additional industry counterexamples are
being recorded in sources.json; these documentation observations are not native
passes.

# Execution, resources and cohort probe plan

Status: plan reviewed by root on 2026-11-22; bounded implementation and strict TypeScript checking authorized, no new runtime executed yet. Root source review requested a bounded cleanup checkpoint and asserted final close reports/physical exits; both were added. State lane peer review and one-package typecheck precede local execution. This adds evidence to Resources6/ALS5/SDK14; those results remain historical evidence, not new test counts.

## Question and selected policy

Can a prepared replacement execute an actual new TS implementation and dependency cohort, while an admitted operation retains its old cohort, and can we separately prove old execution has stopped and old writes are rejected?

Selected test policy: a request admitted to A may finish computation or a read/stream using A after B is published. Publication of B revokes A's authority to commit shared mutable state. This is an explicit policy choice; another host may drain all writes before publication. The adapter must not silently choose for the host.

## Existing mechanisms versus coordination

| Owner | Reused mechanism | Guarantee exercised | Does not provide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Node | `Worker`, literal entry URL, ESM imports, `MessagePort`, `terminate()`/`exit` | Separate real execution contexts and module graphs; termination completion observable in parent | Publication, tenant authorization, database fencing, rollback of dispatched host effects |
| `@get-modular/resources` 0.2.2 | Public `createScope`, `resources.setup`, `control.close`, `CloseReport` | Own started acquisition, register cleanup, preserve late-acquisition custody, report cleanup debt | Borrower admission, graph/cohort selection, a process supervisor, physical-stop proof unless cleanup actually waits for it |
| State fixture | PostgreSQL transaction and narrow typed authority API | Commit/reconcile a selected cohort; receiver checks old effect authority | Executing/loading plugin code or restoring worker heap |
| Parent test | Explicit prepared A/B handles and barrier order | End-to-end composition of those mechanisms and independently asserted receipts | Production generation registry/kernel, dependency solver, generic RPC framework |

The published Resources README and archived Resources6 already show repeated `close()` retries only failed cleanup entries after a settled incomplete flight. We will verify the exact published implementation, then exercise debt with a real worker. A missing or different retry contract must remain visible debt, not be compensated with a custom retry loop masquerading as library behavior.

## Keep five identities separate

| Identity | Meaning and lifetime |
| --- | --- |
| `artifactDigest` | Hash of immutable entry and dependency bytes; two worker instances can run the same artifact |
| `cohortDigest` | Immutable set of artifact/dependency identities selected together; fixture computes a deterministic manifest hash, not a dependency resolver |
| `generationId` | One live worker instance; restart from the same artifact creates a new generation |
| `effectEpoch` | Authority under which an operation may commit a receiver-side mutation; distinct field even if this fixture initially advances it with publication |
| `revision` | PostgreSQL publication record concurrency token, encoded as an exact decimal string |

An operation captures its admitted generation, cohort and authority token once. Its later write must use that captured token, never refresh to the current head merely to pass the guard. An attempt ID identifies a publication retry; an effect ID identifies a mutation retry. Neither is a generation ID.

## Narrow fixture seams

State agent owns these experimental DB primitives (names may be finalized by that lane):

- `readHead()`.
- `admitAttempt({ attemptId, expectedRevision, expectedGeneration, targetGeneration, cohortDigest, baselineId })`: persist exact immutable inputs, reject same-ID/different-input reuse.
- `publishAttempt(attemptId)`: atomic head CAS and committed/conflict durable outcome; same-attempt replay returns the original outcome.
- `observeAttempt(attemptId)`: recorded pending/committed/conflict or unknown.
- `guardedWrite({ effectId, generation, effectEpoch, stateSchema, value })`: committed, stale, or same-effect replay. A committed effect replay after cutover returns the original receipt when exact inputs match. The operation's original authority is retained for the delayed parent-owned request.

Execution lane proposes one small fixture handle, kept outside any public production SPI:

- `prepareWorker({ generationId, artifact, scope })`: acquire a literal A/B worker in `resources.setup`; wait for its validated ready message, return the handle.
- `beginComputation({ operationId, admission })`: send a typed message to that exact worker; receive a first result and a parent-controlled continuation barrier.
- `continueComputation(operationId)`: receive final result from the same worker and dependency.
- `requestHostWrite({ operationId, effectId, admission, value })`: emit a message; the parent captures the original envelope and dispatches the DB operation after a separate test barrier.
- `close()` is the Resources scope operation; cleanup awaits `worker.terminate()` and observes `exit`. No homegrown stop receipt is issued before that event.

Transport is fixture-only structured data with validation at the `unknown` message boundary. No returned closure, cross-worker resource object, transferable state claim, or general RPC package is needed for this slice.

## Decisive scenarios

1. **Actual code and full cohort replacement.** A entry imports A dependency; B entry imports B dependency and uses different computation. Record source hashes. Pause admitted A between two dependency calls, publish B in PostgreSQL, start B work, resume A. Assert literal independent A/A and B/B outputs and immutable IDs, not just a changed configuration tag. No dynamic shared service lookup is used mid-operation.
2. **Irrevocable host request outlives guest.** A emits a host mutation envelope which the parent captures before termination. Publish B, close A and wait for native `exit`, then release the parent-owned request. Guarded receiver rejects A's exact stale token. An intentionally unguarded receiver negative control shows the already-dispatched host action can still commit after physical worker exit. Stopping the guest is not accepted as a write fence.
3. **Cancellation versus completed stop.** Observe native terminate Promise and exit order, and ensure no completion receipt appears merely from an abort request or abandoned close waiter. Do not rely on JavaScript `finally` executing inside a forcibly stopped worker.
4. **Cleanup debt has live consequences.** Inject one cleanup failure before actual `terminate`. A settled incomplete report must coexist with a still-live worker capable of answering a message. If published contract permits retry, a later `close` must actually terminate and clear only that debt; count distinct physical exits. This is additional proof beyond the prior listener-only debt test.
5. **Bound retention by physical ownership.** Exercise at most two simultaneously live worker generations under an explicit test policy. While A remains retained for a stream, B is active; admission of C is refused before acquiring another worker. After A's physical close, C can prepare. The oracle counts actual worker creation and exit receipts. No memory/RSS/GC leak bound or fleet policy is inferred.

Do not add another synthetic 250-listener loop, reimplement the previous late-file acquisition case, or claim database durability from an in-memory compare-and-swap.

## Build, running and review gates

- Maintained sources are ordinary strict `.ts`, compiler TypeScript >=7.0.2. Inspect exact resolved compiler and any tooling dependency before execution; no old embedded TS.
- Use root-approved Node >=24.18.0 and <25 (or supported >=26.10.0 <27) with exact version recorded. Pin Resources 0.2.2 and public tarball integrity; do not deep-import its source or private lifecycle-kernel.
- Align to the state lane's one backend package: strict TypeScript 7.0.2 `noEmit` first, then Node 24.22.3 native `.ts` stripping and built-in test runner. Files assemble into `state/probe/execution`; no second package/lock, transpiler or compiler dependency.
- Separate deterministic local execution from hosted PostgreSQL integration. A locally passing worker test is not the DB E2E.
- Typecheck, tests, exact dependency lock, source manifest hashes, runtime identity and raw receipts are retained. The root decides hosted workflow ownership and archive assembly.
- Original estimate: 5-7 `.ts` files, about 300-450 maintained lines. Source review version has 9 files and roughly 500 lines because transport boundary validation and local/DB suites are separate. There is no production runtime package, graph loader, RPC framework or supervisor. If these responsibilities grow, reduce the fixture rather than invent infrastructure.

## Source-only work in parallel

Inspect and record current/pinned .NET collectible contexts and real reclamation failures; OSGi multi-reference binding semantics; OTP code-load/upgrade restrictions not already covered; Piscina worker-task contract; public Resources versus private lifecycle-kernel availability. Findings must state source-inspected, historically reported, proposed or executed. Native Effect remains its own typed scoped profile; no Promise adapter or new Effect execution is planned by this lane.

Reuse evaluation is narrow: Piscina's bounded-task pool, native Worker lifetime, and Comlink endpoint RPC are different responsibilities. Piscina abortable tasks do not share workers; an aborted task's rejection still precedes physical thread exit. Default sync atomics pauses detached async work between tasks. Comlink 4.4.2's public proxy release is not an awaitable drain/termination receipt; released-source and upstream fixes/issues must be distinguished. Do not install these alternatives collectively or build a custom RPC/supervisor to compensate.

## Explicit exclusions

No sandbox guarantee for Node Workers, no arbitrary ESM graph resolver, no coherent cohort guarantee across independent externally hot-swapped services, no heap restoration on restart, no arbitrary plugin cleanup guarantee, no native Effect execution evidence, no Wasm backend execution, no production-ready standalone library claim.

The held operation uses a real async generator inside the Worker resumed by two explicit messages; it does not qualify Node Readable/HTTP/SSE transport stream behavior. The fixture artifact digest hashes the entry source; its cohort manifest also hashes the literal dependency, driver and protocol sources. These known files are evidence inputs, not a new manifest standard.
